````EDIT (brief.md) <0>
The printing press, perfected by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440, shattered the bottleneck that had kept knowledge locked inside the hands of scribes, monasteries, and elite patrons for over a millennium. Before movable type, a single book could cost as much as a house and take months to copy by hand; after, thousands of identical copies could be produced in days. The result was a flood of printed material—Bibles, legal codes, scientific treatises, pamphlets, and eventually newspapers—that made literacy not just possible but economically rational for the first time, transforming education from a privilege of the few into a shared infrastructure of entire societies.

The press also rewired the architecture of thought itself. Standardized texts meant that scholars in different cities could argue from the same pages, errors could be corrected in later editions, and ideas could travel faster than their authors. The Protestant Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and the Enlightenment all depended on this new capacity to disseminate, debate, and revise ideas at scale. In political terms, a literate public that could read pamphlets and newspapers became harder to govern by decree, seeding the expectations of transparency and representation that would later fuel revolutions.

In the end, the printing press was less a machine than a multiplier: it took whatever ideas a society already possessed—religious, scientific, political, commercial—and amplified them until they reshaped the society itself. Every subsequent information revolution, from the telegraph to the internet, has been a further multiplication of the same fundamental shift: knowledge as a shared, reproducible resource rather than a scarce, hand-copied one.
````
